report.source_text: Imaging studies included a normal chest X-ray, along with abdominal and pelvic ultrasound findings that were also unremarkable. A head and neck computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a multilobulated hyperdense ulcerative scalp lesion located on the right frontal region of the scalp, measuring 9 × 7.8 × 6 cm. Notably, there was no skull bone erosion, and no intracranial extension of the mass was observed. Enlarged bilateral cervical lymph nodes were seen at levels I and II. Additionally, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine showed a pathological compression fracture of the T10 vertebral body with no stenosis of the canal, raising a high suspicion for vertebral metastasis (Fig. 2).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 49-year-old female of African origin presented with a longstanding (>10 years) scalp mass initially non-progressive but recently excised without histopathology. The lesion recurred within 5 months, enlarged, ulcerated, and bled easily. Physical examination showed two scalp masses on the right side: a larger 9x7 cm fungating, tender, bleeding lesion and a smaller 3x3 cm lesion. Biopsy of the lesion was ordered. Baseline labs were normal. Imaging revealed a multilobulated hyperdense ulcerative scalp lesion without skull bone erosion or intracranial extension, enlarged bilateral cervical lymph nodes (levels I and II), and a pathological compression fracture at T10 vertebra suspicious for vertebral metastasis. Although direct histopathology report excerpts confirming mucoepidermoid carcinoma were not sourced, the final diagnosis as per case information is biopsy-confirmed mucoepidermoid carcinoma.
